explain.say: In 1957 the Sydney Opera House was estimated at about seven million Australian dollars. When it opened in 1973 it had cost a hundred and two million. Good estimating aims to avoid surprises like that. Estimates sharpen as a design develops, through these stages.

explain.say: At the heart of a detailed estimate is the bill of quantities: every item measured by strict rules. Take foundations: twelve pad footings, each two metres by two by zero point seven five. That is three cubic metres each, thirty six in all. Why measure by fixed rules rather than each estimator's own way?

explain.say: So every contractor prices exactly the same thing! Each item then gets a unit rate. Look at the build-up for a cubic metre of concrete: materials ninety five dollars, labour thirty, plant ten, overheads and profit fifteen. That is a hundred and fifty dollars a cubic metre, so the footings cost five thousand four hundred.

Now the summary. Excavation, concrete, reinforcement and formwork add up to thirteen thousand eight hundred and twenty dollars. On top goes a contingency, here ten percent, for the unknowns hiding in the ground. The total is fifteen thousand two hundred. Which item costs the most?

explain.say: Concrete! Reinforcement is priced by weight. A handy rule: a steel bar weighs its diameter in millimetres squared, over one hundred and sixty two, in kilograms per metre. A twelve millimetre bar weighs about zero point eight nine. Well done! Challenge: how much does a metre of sixteen millimetre bar weigh?

faq.q: What is a bill of quantities?
faq.a: A document listing every item of work in a project, measured in standard units by a set method, such as NRM2 in the UK or IS 1200 in India, so contractors can price the same work.
asks: What is a BOQ in construction?

faq.q: How is a unit rate built up?
faq.a: From the cost of materials, labour and plant to do one unit of work, plus overheads and profit. Ninety five plus thirty plus ten plus fifteen gives 150 dollars per cubic metre of concrete.

faq.q: What are the stages of a construction cost estimate?
faq.a: A concept estimate from cost per square metre, an elemental estimate by building element, a detailed estimate from a bill of quantities, tender prices from contractors, and finally the final account.

faq.q: How do you calculate the weight of a steel bar?
faq.a: Use d squared over 162 kilograms per metre, with d in millimetres. It comes from steel's density of 7,850 kilograms per cubic metre. A 12 millimetre bar weighs about 0.89 kilograms per metre.
asks: How do you calculate the weight of reinforcement bars?

faq.q: What is a contingency in a cost estimate?
faq.a: An allowance, often 5 to 15 percent, added for risks and unknowns such as poor ground or design changes. It shrinks as the design and site become better known.

facts: The Sydney Opera House was estimated at about A$7 million in 1957 and cost about A$102 million by 1973.
The bar mass rule d²/162 kg/m comes from 7,850 kg/m³ × π/4 × d².
